title: Gravitation
description: Class 9 Physics Gravitation: universal law of gravitation, value of G and g, free fall, mass vs weight, and thrust, pressure & buoyancy (Archimedes' principle) with notes, diagrams, solved examples and tests.

topics.title: Universal Law of Gravitation & g
topics.concept:
Why do things fall? Long before Newton, people knew apples drop and rivers flow downhill, but nobody could explain why the Moon does not fall to Earth the way an apple does. Newton's brilliant leap was to realise that the same force pulls the apple down and keeps the Moon in orbit. He called it gravitation, and he stated it as a single rule that works for any two objects in the universe.

Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation: Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force that is (a) directly proportional to the product of their masses, and (b) inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. In symbols:

  • $F \propto m_1 m_2$ — double either mass and the force doubles.
  • $F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$ — double the distance and the force falls to one-quarter (the inverse-square law).

Combining these gives the famous equation $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, where $G$ is the universal gravitational constant. Its value, measured by Henry Cavendish, is $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. Because $G$ is so tiny, the pull between everyday objects is far too weak to feel — gravitation only becomes obvious when at least one body (like a planet) is enormous.

Acceleration due to gravity ($g$): When Earth pulls a freely falling object, the object accelerates. This acceleration is given the special symbol $g$, and near Earth's surface $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ (often rounded to $10\ \text{m/s}^2$ for quick calculations). Crucially, $g$ does not depend on the falling object's mass — a feather and a coin fall with the same $g$ in a vacuum.

How $g$ is linked to the law: Put the falling object of mass $m$ at Earth's surface. The gravitational pull is $F = \dfrac{G M m}{R^2}$, where $M$ is Earth's mass and $R$ its radius. But this force also equals $mg$ (force = mass × acceleration). Setting them equal, the $m$ cancels and we get $g = \dfrac{G M}{R^2}$. This single result explains a lot: $g$ depends only on the planet's mass and radius, not on the object dropped.

Why $g$ varies:

  • Altitude: higher up, $r$ increases, so $g$ decreases.
  • Depth: deep inside Earth only the mass below pulls, so $g$ decreases, reaching zero at the centre.
  • Shape: Earth is flattened at the poles, so $g$ is largest at the poles ($\approx 9.83$) and smallest at the equator ($\approx 9.78\ \text{m/s}^2$).

The same law explains the orbits of planets and why a satellite stays up: it keeps ‘falling’ toward Earth but moves sideways fast enough to miss it.

examples.problem: State Newton's universal law of gravitation and write its mathematical form, naming every symbol.
examples.solution:
1. The law: every object attracts every other object with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
  2. In symbols, $F \propto m_1 m_2$ and $F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$.
  3. Combining, $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.
  4. Here $F$ = gravitational force, $m_1, m_2$ = the two masses, $r$ = distance between their centres, $G$ = universal gravitational constant $= 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$.

Answer: $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, the inverse-square law of gravitation.

examples.problem: Two bodies of masses $50\ \text{kg}$ and $80\ \text{kg}$ are placed $2\ \text{m}$ apart. Find the gravitational force between them. (Take $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. Write the formula: $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.
  2. Substitute: $F = \dfrac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(50)(80)}{(2)^2}$.
  3. Numerator: $6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4000 = 2.668 \times 10^{-7}$.
  4. Divide by $r^2 = 4$: $F = \dfrac{2.668 \times 10^{-7}}{4} = 6.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{N}$.

Answer: $F \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{N}$ — an extremely small force, which is why we never feel the pull between ordinary objects.

examples.problem: The gravitational force between two objects is $F$. What happens to the force if the distance between them is doubled, all masses unchanged?
examples.solution:
1. Force depends on distance as $F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$.
  2. New distance $= 2r$, so new force $F' \propto \dfrac{1}{(2r)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4r^2}$.
  3. Therefore $F' = \dfrac{1}{4} F$.

Answer: The force becomes one-quarter of the original (the inverse-square law).

examples.problem: Show that the acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface is $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, and hence find $g$. (Take $M = 6 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$, $R = 6.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$.)
examples.solution:
1. An object of mass $m$ at the surface feels $F = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$.
  2. This same force gives it acceleration $g$, so $F = mg$.
  3. Equate: $mg = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$; cancel $m$ to get $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.
  4. Substitute: $g = \dfrac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(6 \times 10^{24})}{(6.4 \times 10^{6})^2}$.
  5. Numerator $= 4.0 \times 10^{14}$; denominator $= 4.096 \times 10^{13}$.
  6. $g = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{14}}{4.096 \times 10^{13}} \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Answer: $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2} \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, independent of the falling object's mass.

examples.problem: If both masses are tripled and the distance between them is also tripled, by what factor does the gravitational force change?
examples.solution:
1. Original: $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$.
  2. New masses $3m_1$ and $3m_2$ give a numerator factor of $3 \times 3 = 9$.
  3. New distance $3r$ gives a denominator factor of $(3)^2 = 9$.
  4. New force $F' = \dfrac{G(3m_1)(3m_2)}{(3r)^2} = \dfrac{9}{9} \cdot \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2} = F$.

Answer: The force is unchanged (the factor of 9 on top cancels the factor of 9 on the bottom).

examples.problem: A planet has twice Earth's mass and twice Earth's radius. Find the value of $g$ on this planet compared with Earth's $g$.
examples.solution:
1. Surface gravity: $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.
  2. For the planet, $M' = 2M$ and $R' = 2R$.
  3. $g' = \dfrac{G(2M)}{(2R)^2} = \dfrac{2GM}{4R^2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{GM}{R^2} = \dfrac{g}{2}$.
  4. With Earth's $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, the planet's $g' = 4.9\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Answer: $g' = \dfrac{g}{2} = 4.9\ \text{m/s}^2$.

recap: Newton's law: $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$ — force grows with the product of masses and falls with the square of the distance.
The universal gravitational constant is $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ and is the same everywhere in the universe.
Acceleration due to gravity near Earth is $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ and does not depend on the falling object's mass.
$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ links $g$ to a planet's mass $M$ and radius $R$, not to the dropped object.
$g$ varies: it decreases with altitude and with depth, and is largest at the poles, smallest at the equator.

quiz.q: In $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, if the distance $r$ is halved, the force becomes:
The value of the universal gravitational constant $G$ is about:
The acceleration due to gravity $g$ on a falling stone depends on:
options: the mass and radius of Earth
quiz.explanation: $g = GM/R^2$ depends on the planet, not on the falling object.

quiz.q: Where is the value of $g$ greatest on Earth's surface?
quiz.explanation: Earth is flattened at the poles (smaller $R$), so $g = GM/R^2$ is largest there.

topics.title: Free Fall, Mass & Weight
topics.concept:
What is free fall? When an object falls toward Earth with only gravity acting on it (no push, no air resistance), we say it is in free fall. During free fall the object's velocity keeps increasing at a steady rate — it accelerates. That acceleration is exactly the acceleration due to gravity, $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. A famous demonstration: in a vacuum tube, a feather and a hammer dropped together hit the bottom at the same instant, because both fall with the same $g$ regardless of mass.

Equations of motion under gravity: Free fall is just uniformly accelerated motion with $a = g$. So the three equations of motion you already know become, taking downward as positive:

  • $v = u + gt$
  • $h = ut + \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$
  • $v^2 = u^2 + 2 g h$

Here $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity, $h$ the height (or distance) fallen, and $t$ the time. If an object is simply dropped, $u = 0$, which simplifies these nicely (for example $h = \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$). If an object is thrown upward, take $g$ as a deceleration (negative), and at the highest point $v = 0$.

Mass: The mass of a body is the amount of matter it contains. It is a measure of the body's inertia — how hard it is to change its motion. Mass is measured in kilograms (kg), is a scalar, and is the same everywhere in the universe. A $5\ \text{kg}$ bag of rice is $5\ \text{kg}$ on Earth, on the Moon, or in deep space.

Weight: The weight of a body is the force with which a planet attracts it. Since weight is a force caused by gravity, $W = mg$. Weight is measured in newtons (N), is a vector (it points downward), and changes with location because $g$ changes. A $5\ \text{kg}$ bag weighs about $49\ \text{N}$ on Earth but far less on the Moon.

Mass vs weight — the key contrast:

  • Mass is matter (kg, scalar, constant); weight is a force (N, vector, varies with $g$).
  • Mass can never be zero for a real object; weight can be zero where $g = 0$ (deep space) and feels zero in free fall (the ‘weightlessness’ astronauts feel).

Weight on the Moon: The Moon has much less mass and a smaller radius than Earth, giving it a surface gravity of about $g_{moon} = 1.63\ \text{m/s}^2$, which is close to $\dfrac{1}{6}$ of Earth's $g$. So an object's weight on the Moon is roughly one-sixth of its weight on Earth, even though its mass is unchanged. This is why astronauts can leap so high in lunar footage — same muscles, same mass, but only one-sixth the weight to lift.

examples.problem: A stone is dropped from rest from a tower and falls for $3\ \text{s}$. Find its velocity just before hitting the ground and the height of the tower. (Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. Dropped from rest, so $u = 0$, $t = 3\ \text{s}$, $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
  2. Velocity: $v = u + gt = 0 + 9.8 \times 3 = 29.4\ \text{m/s}$.
  3. Height: $h = ut + \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(3)^2$.
  4. $h = \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(9) = 44.1\ \text{m}$.

Answer: Final velocity $= 29.4\ \text{m/s}$; tower height $= 44.1\ \text{m}$.

examples.problem: A ball is thrown vertically upward with a speed of $20\ \text{m/s}$. How high does it rise, and how long does it take to reach the top? (Take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. Going up, gravity decelerates the ball, so use $g = -10\ \text{m/s}^2$ with $u = 20\ \text{m/s}$.
  2. At the top $v = 0$. Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$: $0 = (20)^2 + 2(-10)h$.
  3. $0 = 400 - 20h \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{400}{20} = 20\ \text{m}$.
  4. Time to top: $v = u + gt \Rightarrow 0 = 20 + (-10)t \Rightarrow t = 2\ \text{s}$.

Answer: Maximum height $= 20\ \text{m}$; time to reach the top $= 2\ \text{s}$.

examples.problem: Distinguish between mass and weight, giving two differences.
examples.solution:
1. Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force on it ($W = mg$).
  2. Mass is measured in kilograms and is a scalar; weight is measured in newtons and is a vector.
  3. Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with $g$ (location).

Answer: Mass = matter (kg, scalar, constant); Weight = force of gravity (N, vector, varies with location).

examples.problem: An object weighs $60\ \text{N}$ on Earth. Find (a) its mass and (b) its weight on the Moon, where $g_{moon} = \dfrac{1}{6} g_{earth}$. (Take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$ on Earth.)
examples.solution:
1. On Earth $W = mg \Rightarrow 60 = m \times 10 \Rightarrow m = 6\ \text{kg}$.
  2. Mass is the same on the Moon, so $m = 6\ \text{kg}$ there too.
  3. Moon's $g = \dfrac{1}{6} \times 10 = 1.67\ \text{m/s}^2$ (approx).
  4. Weight on Moon $= mg_{moon} = 6 \times 1.67 = 10\ \text{N}$ (i.e. $\dfrac{60}{6}$).

Answer: Mass $= 6\ \text{kg}$ (same everywhere); weight on the Moon $= 10\ \text{N}$, one-sixth of its Earth weight.

examples.problem: A stone is dropped from a height of $80\ \text{m}$. Find the time it takes to reach the ground. (Take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. Dropped, so $u = 0$, $h = 80\ \text{m}$, $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
  2. Use $h = ut + \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$.
  3. $80 = \dfrac{1}{2}(10) t^2 = 5 t^2$.
  4. $t^2 = 16 \Rightarrow t = 4\ \text{s}$.

Answer: The stone takes $4\ \text{s}$ to reach the ground.

examples.problem: Why do a coin and a feather, dropped together inside an evacuated (air-free) jar, reach the bottom at the same time?
examples.solution:
1. In free fall the only force is gravity, giving acceleration $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.
  2. This $g$ is the same for every object and does not depend on mass.
  3. In ordinary air, the feather is slowed by air resistance, so it lags behind the coin.
  4. Remove the air (evacuated jar) and there is no air resistance, so both accelerate equally at $g$.

Answer: With no air resistance both fall with the same acceleration $g$, so they land together regardless of mass.

recap: In free fall the only force is gravity, so the acceleration is $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ for every object.
The equations of motion under gravity are $v = u + gt$, $h = ut + \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$, and $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$.
Mass (kg, scalar) is the amount of matter and is the same everywhere; it measures inertia.
Weight is the force of gravity, $W = mg$ (N, vector), and changes with location because $g$ changes.
On the Moon $g$ is about $\dfrac{1}{6}$ of Earth's, so an object weighs one-sixth as much there, though its mass is unchanged.

quiz.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and is constant everywhere; weight changes with $g$.

topics.title: Thrust, Pressure & Buoyancy (Archimedes' Principle)
topics.concept:
Thrust: When a force acts on a surface, the part of the force acting perpendicular (at right angles) to that surface is called thrust. Thrust is simply a force, so its SI unit is the newton (N). Standing on soft sand, your weight acts as thrust pushing down on the ground.

Pressure: What matters for many effects is not the total thrust but how it is spread out. Pressure is the thrust acting per unit area: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N/m}^2$. The same force on a smaller area gives a larger pressure — that is why a sharp knife (tiny edge area) cuts easily, why a camel's broad feet stop it sinking in sand, and why a sharp nail pierces wood while a blunt one does not.

Pressure in fluids: Liquids and gases (together called fluids) exert pressure on the walls and base of their container and on anything submerged in them. Important facts:

  • Fluid pressure acts in all directions, not just downward.
  • Pressure increases with depth — deeper water pushes harder, which is why dam walls are built thicker at the bottom.
  • At the same depth in the same fluid, the pressure is the same in every direction.

Buoyancy (upthrust): When an object is placed in a fluid, the fluid pushes up on it with a force called the buoyant force or upthrust. This is why a bucket feels lighter when lowered into a well, and why we feel lighter in a pool. The buoyant force acts upward and opposes the object's weight.

Archimedes' Principle: When a body is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The upthrust equals $\rho_{fluid} \cdot V_{displaced} \cdot g$. This single idea explains ships, submarines and hot-air balloons.

Density and relative density: Density is mass per unit volume, $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$, with SI unit $\text{kg/m}^3$. Relative density is the ratio of a substance's density to the density of water: $\text{R.D.} = \dfrac{\rho_{substance}}{\rho_{water}}$. Being a ratio, it has no units. Water's density is $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$ ($1\ \text{g/cm}^3$), so mercury (R.D. $= 13.6$) is 13.6 times as dense as water.

Why objects float or sink: Compare the object's density with the fluid's:

  • Density greater than the fluid's → weight beats upthrust → it sinks (an iron nail).
  • Density less than the fluid's → upthrust wins → it floats, sinking only until it displaces its own weight of fluid (a cork, or a hollow steel ship).
  • Densities equal → it floats fully submerged in balance.

examples.problem: A force of $200\ \text{N}$ acts perpendicularly on a surface of area $4\ \text{m}^2$. Find the pressure exerted.
examples.solution:
1. Pressure formula: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$.
  2. Here $F = 200\ \text{N}$ (thrust) and $A = 4\ \text{m}^2$.
  3. $P = \dfrac{200}{4} = 50\ \text{Pa}$.

Answer: The pressure is $50\ \text{Pa}$ (i.e. $50\ \text{N/m}^2$).

examples.problem: Explain why the same person sinks into soft snow while walking in shoes but not while wearing wide skis.
examples.solution:
1. The person's weight (thrust) is the same in both cases.
  2. Pressure $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$ depends on the area in contact with the snow.
  3. Shoes have a small area, so the pressure on the snow is large and the feet sink in.
  4. Skis spread the same weight over a much larger area, so the pressure is small and the snow supports the person.

Answer: Wide skis increase the contact area $A$, lowering the pressure $P = F/A$ so the person does not sink.

examples.problem: A block of metal has a mass of $270\ \text{g}$ and a volume of $100\ \text{cm}^3$. Find its density and its relative density. (Density of water $= 1\ \text{g/cm}^3$.)
examples.solution:
1. Density: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{270}{100} = 2.7\ \text{g/cm}^3$.
  2. In SI units this is $2700\ \text{kg/m}^3$.
  3. Relative density: $\text{R.D.} = \dfrac{\rho_{substance}}{\rho_{water}} = \dfrac{2.7}{1} = 2.7$.
  4. R.D. is a ratio, so it has no units.

Answer: Density $= 2.7\ \text{g/cm}^3$ ($2700\ \text{kg/m}^3$); relative density $= 2.7$ (this is aluminium).

examples.problem: State Archimedes' principle and use it to explain why a huge steel ship floats while a small steel nail sinks.
examples.solution:
1. Archimedes' principle: a body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
  2. A solid nail has high density; it displaces only a little water, so the upthrust is less than its weight and it sinks.
  3. A ship is hollow, so its overall (average) density is much less than water's.
  4. The ship sinks just far enough to displace a weight of water equal to its own weight, so the upthrust balances the weight and it floats.

Answer: Shape matters: the hollow ship displaces enough water for the buoyant force to equal its weight; the dense nail cannot, so it sinks.

examples.problem: An object weighs $50\ \text{N}$ in air and $40\ \text{N}$ when fully immersed in water. Find the buoyant force on it and the weight of water displaced.
examples.solution:
1. The apparent loss in weight equals the buoyant force (upthrust).
  2. Loss in weight $= 50 - 40 = 10\ \text{N}$.
  3. So the buoyant force $= 10\ \text{N}$.
  4. By Archimedes' principle, the weight of water displaced equals this upthrust $= 10\ \text{N}$.

Answer: Buoyant force $= 10\ \text{N}$; weight of displaced water $= 10\ \text{N}$.

examples.problem: A wooden cube of side $10\ \text{cm}$ and density $600\ \text{kg/m}^3$ is placed in water (density $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$). Will it float or sink, and why?
examples.solution:
1. Compare densities: the cube's density is $600\ \text{kg/m}^3$, water's is $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$.
  2. Since the cube's density ($600$) is less than water's ($1000$), it floats.
  3. Physically, the maximum upthrust (when fully submerged) would exceed the cube's weight, so it rises until only part is submerged.
  4. It floats with the fraction submerged $= \dfrac{600}{1000} = 0.6$, i.e. 60% of the cube is under water.

Answer: It floats (its density is less than water's), with about 60% of its volume submerged.

recap: Thrust is the force acting perpendicular to a surface (unit: newton); pressure is thrust per unit area, $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$ (unit: pascal, $\text{N/m}^2$).
The same force gives more pressure on a smaller area — this is why sharp tools cut and wide feet/skis do not sink.
Fluid pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth; submerged objects feel an upward buoyant force.
Archimedes' principle: the upthrust on an immersed body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.
Density $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$; an object floats if its density is less than the fluid's and sinks if it is greater.

quiz.q: A camel walks easily on sand because its broad feet:
options: increase the pressure on the sand
decrease the pressure on the sand
quiz.explanation: A larger contact area $A$ lowers the pressure $P = F/A$, so it does not sink.

quiz.q: According to Archimedes' principle, the upthrust on a submerged body equals the:
quiz.explanation: Upthrust = weight of the fluid displaced by the body.

quiz.q: An object floats in water if its density is:
quiz.explanation: If the object's density is less than the fluid's, the buoyant force can support its weight, so it floats.

questions.q: In $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, the force is inversely proportional to:
questions.explanation: Gravitation follows the inverse-square law, $F \propto 1/r^2$.

questions.q: The value of the universal gravitational constant $G$ is approximately:
Acceleration due to gravity $g$ at Earth's surface is given by:
questions.explanation: Equating $mg = GMm/R^2$ gives $g = GM/R^2$.

questions.q: If the distance between two masses is tripled, the gravitational force becomes:
questions.explanation: $F \propto 1/r^2$, so tripling $r$ gives $1/9$ of the force.

questions.q: During free fall, all objects (ignoring air) fall with the same:
questions.explanation: $g$ is independent of mass, so all objects accelerate equally.

questions.q: A stone dropped from rest has velocity after $3\ \text{s}$ (take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$):
questions.explanation: $v = u + gt = 0 + 10 \times 3 = 30\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from rest; the distance fallen in $2\ \text{s}$ is (take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$):
questions.explanation: $h = \tfrac12 g t^2 = \tfrac12(10)(4) = 20\ \text{m}$.

questions.q: Which quantity is the same on the Earth and the Moon?
questions.explanation: Mass is constant; weight changes with $g$.

questions.q: The weight of a body is:
questions.explanation: Weight is the gravitational force, $W = mg$.

questions.q: On the Moon, an object's weight is about ___ of its Earth weight:
questions.explanation: Moon's $g$ is about $1/6$ of Earth's.

questions.q: The SI unit of weight is the:
questions.explanation: Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

questions.q: Pressure is defined as:
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$.

questions.q: The SI unit of pressure is the:
questions.explanation: $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N/m}^2$.

questions.q: A force of $100\ \text{N}$ on an area of $5\ \text{m}^2$ gives a pressure of:
A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one because it:
questions.explanation: Smaller area means larger pressure for the same force.

questions.q: Archimedes' principle states the upthrust equals the:
questions.explanation: Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced.

questions.q: An object floats in water if its density is:
questions.explanation: Lower density than the fluid means it floats.

questions.q: Relative density is the ratio of a substance's density to that of:
questions.explanation: R.D. $= \rho_{substance}/\rho_{water}$ and has no units.

questions.q: Fluid pressure ___ as depth increases.
questions.explanation: Deeper fluid columns press harder, so pressure increases with depth.

questions.q: An object weighs $40\ \text{N}$ in air and $35\ \text{N}$ in water. The buoyant force is:
questions.explanation: Apparent loss in weight $= 40 - 35 = 5\ \text{N}$ is the upthrust.

imo.title: IMO / Olympiad Level Test — Chapter 3: Gravitation

questions.q: If both masses are doubled and the distance between them is halved, the gravitational force becomes:
questions.explanation: Masses give $2\times2 = 4$; halving $r$ gives $1/(1/2)^2 = 4$; total $4 \times 4 = 16$.

questions.q: A planet has the same mass as Earth but half its radius. Its surface $g$ compared with Earth's is:
questions.explanation: $g = GM/R^2$; halving $R$ gives $1/(1/2)^2 = 4$ times the value.

questions.q: A ball thrown up returns to the thrower's hand. Its displacement and the sign of acceleration during the upward trip are:
questions.explanation: Over the full flight displacement is zero; gravity acts downward the whole time.

questions.q: A stone dropped from rest falls $H$ in the last second of an $n$-second fall is largest because:
options: the stone covers more distance each second as it speeds up
questions.explanation: Under constant $g$, distance per second increases as velocity builds up.

questions.q: An astronaut's mass is $70\ \text{kg}$. On a planet where $g = 25\ \text{m/s}^2$, the astronaut's weight is:
questions.explanation: $W = mg = 70 \times 25 = 1750\ \text{N}$.

questions.q: Two cubes of equal mass but different volumes are dropped in water; the one that floats higher is the one with:
questions.explanation: Same mass, larger volume means lower density, so it floats higher.

questions.q: A block of relative density $0.8$ floats in water. The fraction of its volume above the surface is:
questions.explanation: Submerged fraction $= 0.8$, so $1 - 0.8 = 0.2$ is above the surface.

questions.q: A liquid has relative density $1.25$. Its density in SI units is:
Why does the same nail sink in water but a needle can rest on the surface only due to surface tension, not buoyancy? Because for the nail:
options: density is greater than water's so weight exceeds upthrust
questions.explanation: The nail's density exceeds water's, so its weight beats the buoyant force.

questions.q: A body of volume $200\ \text{cm}^3$ is fully immersed in water. The buoyant force on it is (take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, $\rho_w = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$):
questions.explanation: $V = 200\ \text{cm}^3 = 2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3$; upthrust $= \rho V g = 1000 \times 2\times10^{-4} \times 10 = 2\ \text{N}$.

questions.q: A stone takes $4\ \text{s}$ to reach the ground when dropped from a cliff. The cliff's height is (take $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$):
Where would a given object weigh the most?
questions.explanation: $g$ is largest at the poles (smallest $R$), so weight is greatest there.

questions.q: A hydrometer floats deeper in a liquid of:
questions.explanation: In a less dense liquid more volume must be submerged to get enough upthrust, so it floats deeper.

questions.q: An object is in 'weightlessness' inside a freely falling lift because:
options: both the object and the lift accelerate downward at $g$, so the floor exerts no normal force
questions.explanation: In free fall the support force vanishes, giving the sensation of weightlessness; mass and $g$ are unchanged.
